report:
## Summary of Evidence

The claim has modest support, but the evidence base is thin and mixed rather than definitive.

**Key trial:** The most cited study is Manber et al. (2010), a randomized controlled trial of 150 pregnant women meeting DSM-IV criteria for depression, comparing depression-specific acupuncture to control acupuncture and massage. Depression-specific acupuncture produced significantly greater symptom reduction and higher response rates (63.9%) than control acupuncture (37.5%), while massage (a second active control) also performed well (50.0%) and didn't differ significantly from either acupuncture arm (https://med.stanford.edu/news/all-news/2010/02/acupuncture-lessens-depression-symptoms-during-pregnancy-study-shows.html; https://journals.lww.com/greenjournal/Abstract/2010/03000/Acupuncture_for_Depression_During_Pregnancy__A.7.aspx). This suggests specificity of acupuncture points matters, but the overlap with massage raises questions about how much benefit is acupuncture-specific versus general relaxation/attention effects.

**Broader literature:** A review by Marc et al. found only a handful of small studies on antenatal acupuncture, calling results "promising" but preliminary (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4758005/). Qualitative work suggests patients and clinicians are open to it but want more safety/efficacy data before mainstream adoption (Flinders University research). For related postpartum depression, network meta-analyses and reliability assessments conclude evidence is inadequate—studies are small, heterogeneous, often lack sham controls, and are prone to publication bias (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11423827/; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9329701/).

**Conclusion:** Acupuncture shows a plausible, moderate benefit for antenatal depression in one well-designed but singular trial, comparable to conventional treatment response rates. However, given the small number of trials, small samples, and inconsistent control comparisons, the claim is "supported by preliminary evidence" rather than firmly established. More rigorous, adequately powered trials with sham controls are needed before treating this as settled science.
